overview: Amargasaurus cazaui was a distinctive Early Cretaceous diplodocoid sauropod from Argentina (~130 Ma), with two parallel rows of tall neural spines running along its neck and back — the most dramatic spinal ornamentation of any sauropod. The spines could have supported a sail-like skin web, individual keratinous spines like a porcupine, or simply been covered in muscle — no soft-tissue evidence directly confirms which.

At around nine metres Amargasaurus was modest-sized for a sauropod, making it more manoeuvrable than the giant Morrison Formation species. Its discovery in 1991 provided important information about the Early Cretaceous sauropod fauna of South America, a continent increasingly isolated from other landmasses as Pangaea continued to break apart.

articles.title: Discovery
articles.body: Leonardo Salgado and José Bonaparte described Amargasaurus cazaui in 1991 from a nearly complete specimen found near the La Amarga stream in Neuquén Province. The spectacular neck spines — reaching up to 60 cm above the vertebrae — were immediately recognised as unique among sauropods.

articles.title: Function of the spines
articles.body: Three main hypotheses: (1) a skin-covered sail for thermoregulation and/or display, analogous to Ouranosaurus; (2) individually keratinous spines forming a porcupine-like defensive array; (3) heavily muscled bases for neck movement control. Finite element analysis suggests the spines could not have been actively moved; the sail or defensive array hypotheses are currently most discussed. No direct soft-tissue evidence has been found.

articles.title: Ecological context
articles.body: The La Amarga Formation records a period when South America was becoming more isolated. Amargasaurus is a dicraeosaurid — a family with long neural spines also known from Tanzania (Dicraeosaurus) — suggesting earlier global distribution of this lineage before continental separation. The Early Cretaceous Patagonian fauna included smaller dinosaurs and crocodylomorphs alongside the larger sauropods.

record.description: Amargasaurus cazaui was a dicraeosaurid sauropod from the La Amarga Formation of Argentina. One partial skeleton preserves much of the vertebral column, including paired, extremely tall cervical neural spines, plus skull and limb elements.
facts: The holotype is relatively complete for a dicraeosaurid but is not a full articulated skeleton.
The neural spines supported soft tissue, but competing sail, sheath and display reconstructions are not decisively resolved.

presentation.heroLead: A short-necked sauropod from Early Cretaceous Argentina whose neck vertebrae carried paired spines taller than any other known dinosaur's, known from one good partial skeleton.

animalParagraphs: Amargasaurus was a small sauropod by the standards of its group, probably around nine to ten metres long. It belonged to the dicraeosaurids, a family of diplodocoid sauropods with unusually short necks that appear to have browsed at low to moderate heights rather than reaching high into the canopy.

Its defining feature is the neck. Each cervical vertebra carried a pair of extremely elongate neural spines that projected upwards and backwards, forming two rows along the neck that continued, at lower height, over the back. Bone microstructure suggests the spines were covered in a hard sheath, but whether they supported a skin sail, a keratin cover or something else is still argued, and their function is unknown.

The skull is only partly preserved, but the braincase shows that the head was habitually held with the snout angled downwards, consistent with low browsing. Its peg-like teeth, inferred from close relatives, would have stripped rather than chewed vegetation.
animalHighlights: Paired neural spines on the neck vertebrae are the tallest known for any sauropod relative to body size.
A short neck for a sauropod, typical of dicraeosaurids, suggests feeding close to the ground.
Braincase anatomy indicates the head was carried with the snout angled downwards.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.reason: Herbivory is not in doubt for a sauropod, and the downward-angled head supports low browsing. Preserved teeth are few, so tooth form leans on dicraeosaurid relatives.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.level: Supported by limb and girdle bones
lifeCards.reason: Fore- and hindlimb elements are preserved and show the columnar four-legged stance of all sauropods.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Length is scaled from the single partial skeleton; mass estimates of around two to three tonnes are model-based and vary between studies.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Histology shows the spines bore a hard covering, but a sail, keratin sheath or fleshy ridge remain competing reconstructions.

presentation.classificationSummary: Amargasaurus is a dicraeosaurid, a family of short-necked diplodocoid sauropods known otherwise from Africa, North America and other South American finds. Its close relationship with Dicraeosaurus and the newer Bajadasaurus is well supported, though the exact branching order within the family shifts between analyses.

related.reason: The African dicraeosaurid that gives the family its name, with shorter neck spines.
An even shorter-necked dicraeosaurid from Jurassic Patagonia.
Compare with a long-necked diplodocoid cousin of the more familiar body plan.

questions.title: What covered the neck spines?
questions.copy: Bone histology shows a hard outer covering, but a skin sail, horn-like sheaths and a fleshy crest have all been proposed. No soft tissue is preserved to settle the question.

questions.title: What were the spines for?
questions.copy: Display, defence, thermoregulation and species recognition have all been suggested. None can be tested directly from a single skeleton.

questions.title: How variable was the species?
questions.copy: Almost everything known rests on one individual, so differences between ages, sexes or individuals cannot be assessed.

review.ageReviewNote: The Puesto Antigual Member of the La Amarga Formation is Barremian-early Aptian.

specimens.name: Holotype
specimens.institution: Museo Argentino de Ciencias Naturales, Buenos Aires
specimens.note: Partial associated skeleton with partial skull, including the braincase, most of the presacral vertebral column, sacrum, anterior caudals, pelvis and limb elements.

panel.headline: One partial skeleton with much of the spectacular neck preserved.
panel.standfirst: Amargasaurus rests almost entirely on the holotype skeleton collected in 1984 from the La Amarga Formation. It preserves part of the skull, most of the neck and back, the sacrum, some tail vertebrae and elements of the girdles and limbs.

coverage.label: Good
coverage.basis: Most skeletal regions are represented in one associated skeleton, but the skull is incomplete, the tail is largely missing and only a single individual is known.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: The holotype includes the back of the skull with the braincase, the cervical, dorsal and sacral vertebrae, the first few caudal vertebrae, ribs, the pelvis and elements of the shoulder girdle, forelimb and hindlimb.
knownRemains.note: The snout, most of the tail and the hands and feet are missing or poorly known, so those regions in mounts and diagrams are reconstructed from relatives.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: The posterior part of the skull, including a well-preserved braincase; the snout and lower jaws are largely unknown.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: A near-complete cervical and dorsal series with the tall paired neural spines, the sacrum, anterior caudal vertebrae and ribs.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Pelvic and pectoral girdle elements with forelimb and hindlimb long bones; the hands and feet are poorly represented.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Bone microstructure of the neural spines has been sampled histologically; no skin, sail impressions or gut contents are known.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A short-necked, low-browsing dicraeosaurid whose neck spines carried a hard covering and most likely served in display, with sail and sheath reconstructions still competing.
